title: Unpacking the RAND Survey on Books in English Language Arts Curriculum
author: Curriculum Insight Project
summary: A RAND survey of 3,640 ELA teachers reveals massive variance in book assignment: 41% of students have two or fewer books per year, 10% of middle school classrooms have zero assigned books, but 24% of secondary teachers assign five or more -- meaning book-starved and book-rich classrooms coexist at every demographic level. Demographics play a smaller predictive role than expected; curriculum type is the decisive variable: teachers using publisher-developed 'standards-aligned' (SA) curricula were significantly more likely to assign fewer books, with 57% of heavy SA users assigning only 1-2 books compared to 25% of non-publisher-curriculum teachers. The Curriculum Insight Project argues RAND's analysis is undermined by its reliance on EdReports as a standards-alignment proxy, since EdReports has awarded top marks to book-starved basals (Wonders, Into Reading) while giving middling or no reviews to book-rich, evidence-backed curricula like Bookworms and Fishtank. The real culprit is basals specifically -- not 'standards-aligned curricula' in the abstract -- which dominate market share partly because EdReports certification became a gateway to state-approval lists and district purchasing decisions. The article challenges RAND's call for more research as a 'shameful waste of time': the reading-volume literature is already substantial, Tim Shanahan's defense of passage-centered programs involves a conflict of interest (he co-authored Wonders and Emerge), and the precautionary principle demands whole-book curricula until passage-only instruction is affirmatively shown to cause no harm.
points: Curriculum type -- not school demographics -- is the strongest predictor of whether students read whole books: moving from no publisher curriculum to heavy use of SA publisher materials shifts the '1-2 books per year' rate from 25% to 57%, with SA most-intensive users assigning five or more books only 7% of the time.

EdReports' 'all-green' rating has been awarded to book-starved basal programs (Wonders, Into Reading, MyView, MyPerspectives) that lack independent efficacy studies, while book-rich curricula with stronger evidence bases have received middling or no reviews -- making EdReports a misleading proxy variable in RAND's analysis.

RAND's analysis conflates 'standards-aligned' with 'EdReports-approved' in a way that obscures the real culprit: passage-centered basals that dominate market share partly because state approval lists have been gatekept by EdReports scores.

Tim Shanahan, the most prominent voice defending passage-centered programs, is a co-author of basal curricula (Wonders, Emerge) -- a conflict of interest the field should acknowledge when weighing his arguments against the reading-volume research.

The precautionary principle provides a strong independent case for books: absent positive evidence that passage-only instruction causes no harm to reading skills and stamina, the default should be whole-book curricula -- the existing reading-volume literature already provides sufficient warrant without waiting for new studies.
quotes: Book-starved and book-rich ELA classrooms can both be found in American schools. Predictably, curriculum is an essential influence.

Teachers serving more historically disadvantaged students (i.e., students experiencing poverty, students of color, multilingual learners, and students with disabilities) assigned fewer full books. It's a troubling finding. But again, we need to note the broad range in every subgroup. Demographics aren't destiny.

Attending a 'good school' in an affluent neighborhood does not insulate a student from a book-starved education. Even in classrooms where 50-100% of students have disabilities, you'll find students reading 5+ books per year.

Among teachers using SA materials most intensely, these percentages were 57% [assigning 1-2 books] and 7% [assigning five or more books]. This difference suggests that the patterns of full-book assignment that we observe among teachers using publisher-developed curricula are driven, in large part, by teachers using SA curricula.

Multiple book-starved programs (Wonders, Into Reading, MyView, MyPerspectives) have earned top marks from EdReports. Further, these 'basal' programs lack studies demonstrating their efficacy, individually or as a category.
Asking the field to wait for new research feels like a shameful waste of time and resources. The better course is relying on the research we already have.

The case for books in reading curriculum can rest on the research above -- or simply on the precautionary principle: until there is clear evidence that passage-only curriculum causes no harm to student reading skills and stamina, we should demand curricula with whole books.
